” 35 David also wrote in another place in the Psalms, "You will not let your Holy One see decay."
” 36 For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, died and was laid with his forefathers, and he also decayed.
But the one whom God raised did not see decay.

Therefore, my brothers, know that through Him the good news of the forgiveness of sins is preached to you, 39 and by the law of Moses you could not be freed from sins, but everyone who believes is freed from all sins through Jesus.

Therefore, be careful, lest that which is written in the prophets' book comes upon you 41 “O you who do evil, look, and be amazed, and perish, for I will do a work in your days, ‘a work which if someone mentions it to you, you will not believe.’
” 42 As Paul and Barnabas were going out of the Jewish synagogue, the people begged them that these things might be spoken to them again the next Sabbath.
When the meeting broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, and they spoke to them and persuaded them to continue in the grace of God.
Beginning of preaching among Gentiles through Paul 44 On the next Sabbath, almost the entire city gathered to hear the word of God.
But seeing the crowds, the Jews became jealous and began to speak against what Paul was saying, contradicting him.

Then Paul and Barnabas spoke up boldly, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first, but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, look, we are turning to the Gentiles.
For the Lord has commanded us, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’
” 48 Hearing this, the Gentiles were glad and began to honor the word of God, and as many as were appointed for eternal life believed.
Then the word of the Lord was spread throughout all that region.
But the Jewish leaders incited the devout and honorable women and the prominent men of the city, and they stirred up a riot against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their territory.
Then Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off their feet against them and went to the city of Iconium.
And the disciples were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.
In the city of Iconium, it happened that they went together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed.
But the unbelieving Gentiles stirred up the minds of the believing brothers and caused bitterness.
Paul and Barnabas stayed there for a long time, speaking boldly, relying on the Lord, and He confirmed the word of His grace by allowing them to perform signs and wonders through their hands.
But the people of the city were divided, so many sided with the Jews and many with the apostles.

When the Gentiles and Jews, along with their leaders, rushed toward them to insult them and stone them, 6 then they realized this and fled to the cities of Lystra and Derbe in the region of Lycaonia and the surrounding areas, 7 and began to preach the good news there.
In Lystra and Derbe 8 In the city of Lystra, there sat a man who was disabled in his feet.
He was lame from birth and had never walked.
He was listening to Paul speak.
Paul looked steadily at him and saw that he had faith to be healed, 10 and said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.”
” Then he jumped up and began to walk around.
Seeing this act of Paul, the people said in a loud voice in the Lycaonian language, “The gods have come down to us in human form.”
” 12 They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes because he was the main speaker.
The priest of the temple of Zeus, which was outside their city, wanted to offer sacrifices along with the people by bringing oxen and wreaths to the gates.

But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, and cried out saying, 15 “O good people, what are you doing? We are also human beings, subject to the same joys and sorrows as you, and we bring you the good news so that you turn from these useless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them.
He allowed all nations to go their own ways in past times.
Nevertheless, He continued to testify about Himself by doing good, and by giving you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.
” 18 By saying this, they restrained the people with great difficulty from offering sacrifices for them.
But some Jews came from the cities of Antioch and Iconium and won the crowd over to their side, and they stoned Paul and, thinking he was dead, dragged him out of the city.
But when the disciples gathered around him, he got up and went into the city, and the next day he went with Barnabas to the city of Derbe.

Returning to the city of Antioch in Syria 21 After preaching the good news to the people of that city and making many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, 22 and kept strengthening the minds of the disciples and encouraging them, saying, “We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations.”
” 23 And they appointed leaders for them in every church, and with fasting and prayer, committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.

Then they passed through the region of Pisidia and reached the region of Pamphylia, 25 and after speaking the word in the city of Perga, they came to the city of Attalia, 26 and from there they went by ship to the city of Antioch, where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work that they had completed.
After arriving at the city of Antioch, they gathered the church and reported what great things God had done with them and that He had opened the door of faith for the Gentiles.
And they stayed with the disciples for a long time.
Then some Jewish believers came from the region of Judea and began to teach the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of the prophet Moses, you cannot be saved.

” 2 When Paul and Barnabas had much contention and debate with them, it was decided that Paul and Barnabas and some others from among them should go to the city of Jerusalem to the apostles and church elders regarding this matter.

The church sent them off, and as they passed through the regions of Phoenicia and Samaria, they spoke about the conversion of the Gentiles to Jesus Christ, which caused all the believing brothers to rejoice greatly.
When they reached the city of Jerusalem, the church, the apostles, and the church elders welcomed them with joy, and Paul and Barnabas reported what great things God had done with them.
But some from the sect of the Pharisees who had believed rose up and said, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and ordered to keep the law of the prophet Moses.”
” 6 Then the apostles and church elders gathered to consider this matter.

Then, after much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “O brothers, you know that a long time ago God chose me from among you so that the Gentiles might hear the word of the good news through my mouth and believe.
God, who knows the heart, testified to them by giving them the Holy Spirit just as He did to us, 9 and by purifying their hearts through faith, He made no distinction between us and them.

So why do you test God now, by placing a yoke on the shoulders of the Gentile disciples, which neither our ancestors nor we could bear? 11 Yes, my conviction is that just as they will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, we will also be saved.
” 12 Then the whole assembly began to listen silently to Barnabas and Paul, as they told what great signs and wonders God had shown among the Gentiles through them.
At the conclusion of their speech, James said to the assembly, “Listen to me, O brothers.
” 14 Simon Peter explained how God first looked with mercy on the Gentiles to take from among them a people for His name.

The writings of the prophets also support this, as it is written in the holy scriptures, 16 “After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tabernacle of David, and I will rebuild its ruins, and I will set it up,” 17 so that the rest of humanity may find God, and all those Gentiles upon whom my name has been stamped may seek the Lord, 18 the Lord says this, who has been telling of these things since the beginning of the world.

“Therefore, my opinion is that we should not cause trouble for those Gentiles who are turning to God, we should not distress them, 20 but it would be better for us to write and send them an order that they should abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from sexual immorality, from meat of strangled animals, and from blood.
For from ancient times, there have been those who preach the law of the prophet Moses in every city, and it is read in the synagogue every Sabbath.

” Letter to the Gentile believers 22 Then it seemed good to the apostles and church elders, along with the whole church, to choose some men from among themselves, that is, Judas who is called Barsabbas, and Silas, who were leaders among the brothers, and send them to the city of Antioch with Paul and Barnabas.
They sent this letter by their hands, “Greetings from the apostles and elder brothers to the brothers who are among the Gentiles living in the city of Antioch and in the regions of Syria and Cilicia.
We have heard that some from among us went there and frightened you with their words and turned your minds, but we had not given them such orders.
Because of this, we have unanimously decided it is right to send chosen men to you along with our beloved Barnabas and Paul.
These are men who have risked their lives for the sake of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore, we have sent Judas and Silas, so that you can hear about this from their own mouths.

The Holy Spirit and we have decided not to lay any burden on you other than these necessary things: 29 that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality.
If you abstain from these, it will be well with you.
Everything else is fine.
” 30 Then they departed and reached the city of Antioch, and having gathered the assembly, they gave the letter to them.
They were very glad to read the letter because of its encouraging message.
Judas and Silas, who were also prophets, encouraged the believing brothers with many words and strengthened them.
After staying for a few days, they were sent off in peace by the believing brothers to return to those who had sent them.
(But Silas found it good to stay there.
) 35 But Paul and Barnabas remained in the city of Antioch and, along with many others, continued to teach the word of the Lord Jesus and preach the good news.

Paul's second missionary journey, disagreement between Paul and Barnabas 36 After a few days, Paul said to Barnabas, “Come, let us walk back to all the cities where we preached the word of the Lord and see how our believing brothers are doing.”
” 37 Then Barnabas thought of taking along John who is called Mark.
But Paul did not think it right to take along the one who had separated from them in the region of Pamphylia and had not gone with them for the work.
Finally, there was such a dispute that they separated from each other, and Barnabas took Mark and went by ship to the island of Cyprus.

But Paul chose Silas, and after being committed by the believing brothers to the grace of God, he went away from there, 41 and he traveled through the regions of Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
Then he also went to the cities of Derbe and Lystra.
There was a disciple there named Timothy, whose mother was a Jewish believer, but his father was a Greek.
He had a good reputation among the brothers in the cities of Lystra and Iconium.
Paul's wish was for him to go along with him, and because of the Jewish people who were in those places, he circumcised him, because they all knew that his father was a Greek.
Paul and his companion went from city to city, handing over all the commands that the apostles and church elders of the city of Jerusalem had determined.
In this way, the church became established in the faith and the numbers increased day by day.
Paul's vision in Troas 6 They passed through the regions of Phrygia and Galatia, because the Holy Spirit prevented them from preaching the word in the region of Asia.
Upon reaching the borders of the region of Mysia, they wanted to go into the region of Bithynia, but the Holy Spirit did not let them go.
Finally, they passed through the region of Mysia and came to Troas.
There, at night, Paul had a vision of a man from the region of Macedonia standing and begging him, saying, “Cross over and come into the region of Macedonia, and help us.”
” 10 After he had this vision, we immediately wanted to go to the region of Macedonia, thinking that God had called us to preach the good news to them.
Conversion of Lydia in Philippi 11 Therefore, setting sail from the city of Troas, we went straight to the island of Samothrace and the next day came to the city of Neapolis.
From there we reached the city of Philippi, which is a prominent city in the region of Macedonia and a Roman colony, and we stayed in that city for a few days.
On the Sabbath, we went outside the gate of the city to the riverside, thinking there would be a place for prayer, and sat down and began to talk to the women who had gathered.
A woman named Lydia, a worshiper of God who sold purple fabric from the city of Thyatira, was listening to their talk.
The Lord opened her heart so that she would focus on Paul's words.
When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, “If you consider me a believer in the Lord, then come and stay in my house,” and she prevailed upon us.
Paul and Silas in prison 16 When we were going to the place of prayer, we met a young slave girl who had a spirit of divination, and she used to earn a lot for her masters by predicting the future.
She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are telling us the way of salvation.”
” 18 She kept doing this for many days, but Paul became annoyed, and turning to that unclean spirit, he said, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.”
” And it came out at that very moment.

When her masters saw that the hope of their earnings was gone, they grabbed Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace to the officials, 20 and brought them to the judge and said, “These men, who are Jews, are causing riots in our city, 21 and are telling customs that are not proper for us Romans to adopt.”
” 22 Then the crowd rose up against them, and the authorities tore their clothes off them and gave orders to beat them with rods.
After many beatings, they threw them into prison and gave orders to the jailer to keep them secure.
Receiving such an order, he placed them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in wooden stocks.
Paul and Silas's release from prison 25 At midnight, Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so much so that the foundations of the prison were shaken, and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were released.
The jailer woke up, and seeing the prison doors open, he understood that the prisoners had fled, so he drew his sword and wanted to kill himself.
But Paul called out in a loud voice, 'Don't harm yourself, because we are all here.'

Then the jailer called for lights and went inside, and trembling, fell before Paul and Silas, 30 and brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?' 31 They said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you and your household will be saved.'
32 And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house.
At that very hour of the night, he took them and washed their wounds, and he and all his family were baptized.
Then the jailer took them into his house and set food before them, and he and his whole household rejoiced, having believed in God.
The next day, the magistrates sent the police to say, 'Let those men go.'
The jailer reported these words to Paul, 'The magistrates have ordered that you be released.'
So now go in peace.
37 But Paul said to them, 'They have beaten us publicly without trial, even though we are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison.'
Are they now going to get rid of us secretly? No, let them come themselves and escort us out.

38 The police reported these words to the magistrates, and when they heard that they were Roman citizens, they were afraid, 39 and came and apologized to them, and took them out and requested them to leave the city.
They came out of the prison and went to Lydia's place, and after meeting with the believing brothers, they comforted them and departed.
Paul and Silas traveled through the cities of Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews.

Paul went to them as was his custom, and for three Sabbath days, he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, 3 explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.'
4 And some of the Jews were persuaded, as were a great many of the devout Greeks and a large number of the leading women, and they joined Paul and Silas.

But the Jews, filled with jealousy, gathered some wicked men from the marketplace, formed a mob, and set the city in an uproar, and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the people.
When they did not find them there, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also.'
Jason has welcomed them into his house.
These are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.
8 They stirred up the crowds and the city authorities when they heard these things.
So they released Jason and the others after taking security from them.
10 The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived there, they went into the synagogue of the Jews.
These people were more noble than those in Thessalonica, and they received the word with all eagerness, and examined the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.
Therefore, many of them believed, and also many of the prominent Greek women and men.
But when the Jews of Thessalonica learned that the word of God was being proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds.
Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained at Berea.
Paul's companions brought him as far as Athens, and they departed with a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible.
16 Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers began to argue with him, and some said, 'What does this babbler wish to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities,' because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection.

Then they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, asking, 'May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? 20 For you bring some strange things to our ears; we wish to know therefore what these things mean.'
21 (Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new.)
22 So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said, 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious.'
For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: 'To the unknown god.'
What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.'

24 The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, 25 nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything.

He made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, 27 that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us.
For in him we live and move and have our being; as even some of your own poets have said, 'For we are indeed his offspring.'
29 'Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man.'
The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent.
Because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.'
32 Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, but others said, 'We will hear you again about this.'
33 So Paul went out from their midst.
But some men joined him and believed, among whom were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.
After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.
And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy.
He was with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome.
So he went to see them.
And because he was of the same trade, he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.
And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks, that Jesus was the Christ.
When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Jesus was the Christ.
And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent.'
From now on I will go to the Gentiles.'
7 Paul left the synagogue and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized.

And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, 10 for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.'
11 And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, 13 saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'
14 But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, 'If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint.'
But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves; I refuse to be a judge of these things.'
16 And he drove them from the tribunal.
And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal.
But Gallio paid no attention to any of this.
Returning to Antioch, 18 Paul stayed many days longer in Corinth.
And then, taking leave of the brothers, he sailed to Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila, and at Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.
And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay for a longer period,
21 he declined, but on taking leave of them he said, 'I will return to you if God wills.'
22 And he set sail from Ephesus, and when he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church and went down to Antioch.
Paul's third missionary journey, 23 after spending some time there, he departed and went from place to place through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
Apollos in Ephesus, 24 Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus, competent in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed,
for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Jesus was the Christ.
While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus.
There he found some disciples.
And he said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' And they said, 'No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.'
3 And he said, 'Into what then were you baptized?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.'
4 And Paul said, 'John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.'
5 On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying.
There were about twelve men in all.
And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God.

But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, arguing daily in the hall of Tyrannus.
This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.
And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul,
so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.'
14 Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this.

But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' 16 And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks; and fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled.
Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices.

And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.
Now after these events, Paul resolved in the spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, 'After I have been there, I must also see Rome.'
22 And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
A disturbance in Ephesus, 23 About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way.
For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.
These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, 'Men, you know from this business we have our wealth.'

You see and hear that not only in the city of Ephesus, but almost throughout the whole province of Asia, this Paul has convinced and misled many people by saying that gods made by human hands are not gods.

Now, it is not just that our trade will lose its reputation, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be considered insignificant, and the importance of the one whom all of Asia and the world worship will also be lost.

Hearing this, the craftsmen were filled with rage and began shouting, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' And the whole city was in a commotion; they grabbed Gaius and Aristarchus, who were Paul's traveling companions from Macedonia, and rushed together into the theater.
When Paul wanted to go in among the people, the disciples would not let him.
Even some of the officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to risk going into the theater.
Some were shouting one thing and some another; the whole crowd was completely confused, and most of them did not even know why they had gathered.
Then they brought Alexander forward in the crowd, whom the Jews had pushed ahead.
Alexander made a motion with his hand, wanting to give an account to the people.
But when they realized that he was a Jew, all of them shouted in unison for about two hours, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'

Then the city clerk quieted the crowd and said, 'Men of Ephesus, who does not know that the city of Ephesus is the guardian of the temple of the great goddess Artemis and of the image that fell from Zeus?'
Finally, since these facts cannot be refuted, it is right that you remain calm and do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men who are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
Therefore, if Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen have a grievance against anyone, courts are open, and there are proconsuls; let them bring charges against each other.
But if you want to ask anything else, it will be decided at the legal assembly.
Because of today's incident, we are in danger of being charged with rioting, as there is no solid reason for this, and we will not be able to account for this gathering.
Saying this, he dismissed the assembly.
When the riot had subsided, Paul called the disciples to him, encouraged them, and after taking leave of them, set out for the province of Macedonia.
After passing through all those regions and encouraging the disciples extensively, he came to the country of Greece.
When he had stayed there for three months and was about to sail to Syria from there, the Jewish leaders plotted against him, so he decided to return through the province of Macedonia.

Sopater, son of Pyrrhus from Beroea, and Aristarchus and Secundus from the city of Thessalonica, and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from the province of Asia accompanied him to the province of Asia.
These traveling companions of ours went on ahead and waited for us.
And after the days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi and reached them in Troas in five days, where we stayed for seven days.

In Troas, bringing Eutychus back to life: On the first day of the week, when we gathered for the Lord's Supper, Paul, who was to leave the next day, talked to them and kept on speaking until midnight.
There were many lamps burning in the upstairs room where we were gathered.
And a young man named Eutychus was sitting in a window and began to doze off.
As Paul kept on talking, Eutychus fell into a deep sleep, fell from the third story, and died.
Paul went down, fell upon him, embraced him, and said, 'Do not be alarmed, he is alive.'
And he went up again, broke bread and ate, and continued talking to them until daybreak, then he left.
Then he departed.
And they brought the young man home alive and were greatly comforted.
The journey from Troas to Miletus: We boarded a ship and sailed for the city of Assos, where we were to take Paul aboard; he had traveled by land, as he had planned it that way previously.
When he met us at the city of Assos, we took him on board the ship and arrived at the city of Mitylene.
Setting sail from there, the next day we arrived opposite the island of Chios, and the following day we went towards the island of Samos, and a day after that we reached the harbor of Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past the city of Ephesus rather than stop, because he wanted, if possible, to reach the city of Jerusalem by the day of Pentecost instead of staying in the province of Asia.
Exhortation to the elders of the city of Ephesus: From Miletus, Paul sent word to the city of Ephesus and called for the elders of the church.

When they came to him, he said to them, 'You know how I lived with you at all times from the very first day I arrived in the province of Asia, that is, with great humility, through many tears, and in the midst of trials that came upon me due to the plots of the Jews, I continued to serve the Lord.'

And I never hesitated to tell you whatever was for your benefit, teaching it publicly and from house to house, but I continued to testify to both Jews and Greeks that they must turn to God and have faith in our Lord Jesus.
Now see, I go to the city of Jerusalem, bound by the Holy Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there.
Only that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions are ready for you.

But I do not consider my life of any account as something to be cherished; rather, I want to finish my race and the service which I received from the Lord Jesus to testify to the gospel of God's grace.
And now, I know that you all, among whom I have preached the kingdom of God, will not see my face again.
Therefore, I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of anyone.
For I have never hesitated to tell you the whole will of God.
Therefore, pay attention to yourselves and to the flock over which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, so that you may watch over the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.
I know that after my departure, savage wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock.
Even from among your own selves, men will arise who will speak perverse things to draw away the disciples after them.
Therefore, stay awake, and remember that for three years, night and day, I never stopped warning everyone with tears.
And now I commend you to God and to the word of His grace, which has the power to build you up and give you an inheritance among all those who have been sanctified for the Lord.
I have not coveted anyone's silver, gold, or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands have provided for my needs and those of my companions.

I showed you in every way that by working hard in this manner, it is necessary to help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, which He Himself said: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'
Saying this, he knelt down and prayed with all of them.
Then they all wept bitterly and, embracing Paul, began to kiss him.
They were especially grieved by what he said, that they would not see his face again.
After this, they went with Paul to the ship.
When we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to the island of Cos, the next day to the island of Rhodes, and from there to the island of Patara.
There we found a ship going over to the province of Phoenicia, and we boarded it and began our journey.
When we saw the island of Cyprus to our left, we left it behind and sailed on to the province of Syria and arrived at the city of Tyre, because the ship was to unload its cargo there.
Finding the disciples, we stayed there for seven days.
Through the Holy Spirit, they told Paul not to set foot in Jerusalem.

After seven days, when the time came for us to leave, they all, with their families, came with us to the edge of the city to see us off, and we knelt down on the beach and prayed; then, after saying farewell to one another, we boarded the ship, and they returned to their own homes.
When we finished our voyage from Tyre and arrived at the city of Ptolemais, we greeted the believing brothers and stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left there and came to the city of Caesarea, and we stayed at the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven men chosen by the apostles to serve the widows in Jerusalem.
He had four unmarried daughters who used to prophesy.
As we stayed there for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from the province of Judea.

Coming to us, he took Paul's belt, bound his own hands and feet, and said, 'The Holy Spirit says that the man to whom this belt belongs, the Jews will bind in Jerusalem in this manner and will hand him over to the hands of the Gentiles.'
When we heard this, we and the people there begged Paul not to go to Jerusalem.
But Paul answered, 'Why are you doing this, breaking my heart with your weeping? I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in the city of Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.'
When he would not be persuaded, we remained silent, saying, 'The Lord's will be done.'
After several days, we made preparations and started off for Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us and took us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, one of the original disciples, to stay with him.
Paul's visit with James: When we arrived in Jerusalem, the believing brothers received us with great joy.
The next day Paul went with us to see James, where all the elders of the church were gathered.
After greeting them, he related one by one all the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
Hearing this, they glorified God and said to him, 'Brother, you see that there are many thousands among the Jews who have believed, and they are zealous for all the laws and customs.'
They have heard that you are teaching all the Jews who live among the Gentiles to forsake the law of Moses, and that you tell them not to circumcise their children or walk according to the customs.
So, what is to be done? People will certainly hear that you have come.
Therefore, do what we say to you.
Take our advice; there are four men here who have taken a vow.

Go with them, perform the rite of purification, and pay their expenses for the head-shaving, then everyone will know that there is no truth in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also observe the law.

But regarding the Gentiles who have believed, we have decided and written that they should keep themselves from meat offered to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality.

Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself with them and went into the temple, and there he announced when the days of purification would be completed, that is, the time until the offering was to be made for each of them.

Paul's arrest in the temple: When the seven days were almost over, the Jews from the province of Asia saw Paul in the temple and incited all the people, and seized him with a shout, 'Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everywhere against the people, the law, and this place, and even more, he has brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place.'
For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with Paul, and they thought that Paul had brought him into the temple.
Then the whole city was in a commotion, people ran together, seized Paul, and dragged him out of the temple, and the doors were immediately shut.
While they were trying to kill him, word reached the commander of the garrison that all of Jerusalem was in an uproar.
Then he immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them, and when they saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the commander came up, took Paul, and ordered him to be bound with two chains, and asked, 'Who is this and what has he done?' But some in the crowd were shouting one thing and some another.
Since he could not learn the truth because of the uproar, he ordered him to be taken into the barracks.
When he reached the stairs, it happened that the soldiers had to carry him because of the pressure of the crowd.
For the crowd of people was following, shouting, 'Away with him!'

As they were about to take Paul into the barracks, he said to the commander, 'May I say something to you?' He replied, 'Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian who, some days ago, stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?' Paul said, 'I am a Jew from Tarsus! I am a citizen of Tarsus, a city in the province of Cilicia.'
I beg you, let me speak to the people.
When he gave permission, Paul stood on the stairs and motioned with his hand to the people.
When they became quiet, he began to speak in the Hebrew language: 'Brothers and elders, hear my defense, which I now bring before you.'
When they heard that he was speaking to them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet.

Then he said, 'I am a Jew, born in the city of Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, taught strictly according to the law of our ancestors, and was as zealous for God as you all are today.'
I persecuted this movement to the point of death, binding both men and women and putting them in prison.

The high priest and all the Jewish elders are witnesses to this, from whom I received letters to the brothers and was on my way to the city of Damascus, to bring those who were there bound to Jerusalem to be punished.
Mention of his conversion: 'As I was on my way and approached the city of Damascus, it happened that about noon a great light from heaven shone around me.'
And I fell to the ground and heard this voice, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ He said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’
My companions saw the light, but they did not understand the one who was speaking to me.
Then I said, ‘Lord, what shall I do?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Get up and go into the city of Damascus, and there you will be told everything that has been appointed for you to do.’
When I could not see anything because of the brightness of that light, I came to the city of Damascus, holding the hands of my companions.
Then a devout man named Ananias, according to the law, who was well known among all the Jews living there, came to me and, standing near me, said, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’
At that very moment my eyes opened, and I saw him.
Then he said, ‘The God of our ancestors has appointed you to know His will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear words from His mouth.
For you will be His witness before all people concerning the things you have seen and heard.
Now why are you waiting? Get up, be baptized, and wash away your sins by calling on His name.’

‘While I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I became unconscious and saw Him saying to me, “Hurry and leave Jerusalem immediately, because they will not accept your testimony about me.”
I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that I used to imprison those who believed in you and beat them in one synagogue after another.
When the blood of your witness Stephen was being shed, I too was standing there, agreeing with it and guarding the clothes of those who were killing him.’
And the Lord said to me, ‘Go, because I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’

The people listened to him up to this statement, and then they shouted loudly, ‘Destroy this man; it is not right for him to remain alive!’ As they shouted, threw off their clothes, and threw dust into the air, the commander ordered that he be taken into the fortress and examined by whipping, so that he might find out why the people were shouting against him in this way.

When they tied him with straps, Paul said to the centurion standing nearby, ‘Is it lawful for you to whip a Roman citizen, and that too without finding him guilty?’ When the centurion heard this, he went to the commander and said, ‘What are you doing? This man is a Roman citizen.’
Then the commander came to him and asked, ‘Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?’ He said, ‘Yes.’
The commander replied, ‘I obtained the status of a Roman citizen by paying a large amount of money.’

Paul said, ‘But I am a Roman citizen by birth.’ Then the men who were about to examine him immediately moved away, and the commander also became afraid when he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him.

Paul before the Jewish council: The next day, wanting to know exactly why the Jews were accusing him, he released him from his chains and ordered the chief priests and the Jewish council to assemble. He brought Paul down and made him stand before them.
Paul looked carefully at the Jewish council and said, ‘Brothers, I have lived with a completely sincere conscience before God until this day.’
At this, the high priest Ananias ordered those standing near him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, ‘God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You are sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet, contrary to the law, you order me to be struck.’
Those standing nearby said, ‘Do you insult God's high priest?’
Paul said, ‘Brothers, I did not know that he was the high priest, because it is written, “You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people.”’

Then Paul, knowing that one group consisted of Sadducees and the other of Pharisees, shouted in the council, ‘Brothers, I am a Pharisee, descended from Pharisees. I am on trial concerning the hope of the dead and the resurrection.’
When he said this, a dispute arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided.
For the Sadducees believe that there is no resurrection, no angels, and no spirit, but the Pharisees believe in all these things.

A great uproar arose, and some scribes belonging to the Pharisee group stood up and argued, saying, ‘We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?’ When the uproar became great, the commander feared that they might tear Paul to pieces, so he ordered the soldiers to go down, pull him out from among them by force, and take him into the fortress.
That night the Lord Jesus stood near him and said, ‘Paul, take courage, because just as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, you must also testify in Rome.’
The plot to kill Paul: When day came, the Jews formed a plot and took an oath that they would not eat or drink until they had killed Paul; they called a curse upon themselves if they did.
Those who took this oath together were more than forty men.
They went to the chief priests and Jewish elders and said, ‘We have firmly decided that we will eat nothing until we have killed Paul; may a curse fall upon us if we eat anything before that.’
Therefore, now ask the commander and the Jewish council to bring him down to you, pretending that you want to investigate his case more accurately. We will be ready to kill him before he reaches you.
Paul's nephew heard that they were lying in wait, so he went into the fortress and informed Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions to him and said, ‘Take this young man to the commander, because he has something to tell him.’
So he took him to the commander and said, ‘The prisoner Paul called me and requested that I bring this young man to you, because he has something to tell you.’
The commander took him by the hand, went aside with him, and asked, ‘What do you want to tell me?’
He said, ‘The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul before the Jewish council tomorrow, pretending that they want to examine his case more accurately.

But do not believe them, because more than forty men among them are waiting to kill him. They have taken an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul. They are now ready and are waiting for your permission.’
Then the commander dismissed the young man, ordering him, ‘Do not tell anyone that you have informed me of these things.’
Paul is sent to Felix: Then he called two centurions and said, ‘Prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen to go to Caesarea at nine o'clock tonight.
Also provide horses for Paul to ride, so that he may be taken safely to Governor Felix.’
He also wrote a letter in this manner: ‘Claudius Lysias sends greetings to His Excellency Governor Felix.
This man had been seized by the Jews, who wanted to kill him, but when I learned that he was a Roman citizen, I came with soldiers and rescued him.
I wanted to know the reason why they were accusing him, so I brought him before their Jewish council.
I found that he was being accused concerning questions of their law, but there was no charge against him deserving death or imprisonment.
When I was informed that a plot was being made against this man, I immediately sent him to you and also ordered his accusers to present their charges against him before you.’
So the soldiers carried out their orders and brought Paul by night to Antipatris.
The next day they left the horsemen to continue with him and returned to Jerusalem themselves.
When they reached Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and presented Paul before him.

After reading the letter, the governor asked, ‘From which province is this man?’ When he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said to him, ‘I will hear your case when your accusers also arrive.’ And he ordered that he be kept under guard in Herod's palace.
Five days later, the high priest Ananias arrived in Caesarea with several Jewish elders and a lawyer named Tertullus.
They made accusations against Paul before the governor.
When Paul was called, Tertullus began accusing him, saying, ‘Your Excellency Felix, through you we enjoy great peace, and through your administration many improvements are being made for this nation.
We accept these things with gratitude, everywhere and in every way.
So that I may not take up too much of your time, I request you to hear a few words from us with your kindness.’
‘We have found this man to be a troublemaker, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a leader of the sect of the Nazarenes.
He also tried to defile the temple, so we seized him.
We wanted to judge him according to our law, but Commander Lysias came and took him away from our hands by force and ordered his accusers to come before you.
By examining him yourself, you will be able to learn the truth about all the charges we are bringing against him.’
The Jews also joined in the accusation, saying that these things were true.
Paul's reply: When the governor signaled to Paul to speak, he replied, ‘Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I gladly defend myself before you.
You can find out for yourself that it has been no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship in the temple.
They did not find me arguing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple, in the synagogues, or anywhere in the city.
Nor can they prove to you the charges they are now bringing against me.
But I admit this to you: according to the Way that they call a sect, I worship the God of my ancestors, believing everything written in the Law and the Prophets.
I have hope in God, a hope that they themselves also have, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous.
Because of this, I also try to keep my conscience clear before God and before people at all times.’
‘After many years, I came to bring gifts for the poor and to offer sacrifices.
While I was doing this, they found me in the temple completing the purification ritual. There was no crowd or disturbance. However, some Jews from the province of Asia were there.
If they have anything against me, they should come here before you and make their accusations.

Or let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found in me when I stood before the Jewish council, except for this one statement I shouted while standing among them: “Today I am on trial before you concerning the resurrection of the dead.”’
Felix, who knew the Way quite well, postponed the matter by saying, ‘When Commander Lysias comes, I will decide your case.’
He ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody but to allow him some freedom and to let his friends come and take care of him.
Paul before Felix and Drusilla: Some days later, Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.
As Paul spoke about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became afraid and replied, ‘For now, go away. When I have an opportunity, I will call you again.’
Felix also hoped that Paul would give him some money, so he sent for him more often and talked with him.
After two years had passed, Porcius Festus succeeded Felix, and Felix left Paul in prison because he wanted to please the Jews.
Three days after taking office as governor, Festus went from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
The chief priests and the prominent Jewish men accused Paul before him and asked that he be sent to Jerusalem. In reality, they were planning to kill him along the way.
Festus replied, ‘Paul is being kept under guard in Caesarea, and I myself will go there shortly.’
He said, ‘Let those among you who have authority go with me, and if this man has done anything wrong, let them accuse him.’
After staying among them for about eight or ten days, Festus went down to Caesarea. The next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered Paul to be brought in.
When Paul arrived, the Jewish leaders who had come from Jerusalem stood around him and brought many serious charges that they could not prove.
But Paul defended himself, saying, ‘I have committed no crime against the law of the Jews, the temple, or Caesar.’

Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asked Paul, ‘Are you willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there before me concerning these charges?’ Paul answered, ‘I am standing before Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well.
If I am guilty and have done anything deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if none of their accusations against me is true, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar.’
Then Festus discussed the matter with his council and replied, ‘You have appealed to Caesar; you will go to Caesar.’
Paul before King Agrippa: After some days, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived in Caesarea and paid a visit to Festus.
After they had stayed there for many days, Festus told the king about Paul, saying, ‘There is a man here whom Felix left as a prisoner.
When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the Jewish elders accused him and demanded that he be sentenced.
I replied to them that it is not the Roman custom to hand over any person for punishment before the accused has faced his accusers and has had an opportunity to answer the charges.
When they gathered here, I did not delay. The very next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man to be brought in.
When his accusers stood up, they did not bring any of the accusations I had expected concerning wrongdoing.
Instead, they argued with him about their own religion and about a man named Jesus, who had died but whom Paul claimed was alive.
I was uncertain how to investigate these matters, so I asked him whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there concerning these issues.
But when Paul appealed to have his case decided by the emperor, I ordered him to be kept in custody until I could send him to Caesar.’
Then Agrippa said to Festus, ‘I would also like to hear this man.’
He replied, ‘You will hear him tomorrow.’
The next day Agrippa and Bernice arrived with great ceremony and entered the audience hall with the commanders and the prominent men of the city.
Then Festus ordered Paul to be brought in.

Festus said, ‘King Agrippa, and all the men who are here with us, you see this man about whom all the Jews in Jerusalem and here have repeatedly appealed to me, shouting that he should not remain alive.
But I found that he had done nothing deserving death, and when he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to send him.
Then Agrippa said to Paul, 'You have permission to speak for yourself.'

Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense: 'King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to make my defense before you today concerning all the accusations brought against me by the Jewish leaders, especially because you are well acquainted with all the Jewish customs and controversies.'
Therefore, I beg you to listen to me patiently.
All the Jews know the way I have lived ever since I was young, both in my own country and in Jerusalem.
They have known me for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that I conformed to the strictest sect of our religion, living as a Pharisee.
And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise God made to our ancestors.
This is the promise our twelve tribes are hoping to see fulfilled as they earnestly serve God day and night.
King, it is because of this hope that I am being accused by the Jews.
Why should any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead? I too was convinced that I ought to do all that was possible to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And that is just what I did in Jerusalem. On the authority of the chief priests, I put many of the Lord's people in prison, and when they were put to death, I cast my vote against them.
Many a time I went from one synagogue to another to have them punished, and I tried to force them to blaspheme. I was so obsessed with persecuting them that I even hunted them down in foreign cities.

In this mission, I was on my way to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. About noon, King, as I was on the road, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, blazing around me and my companions.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me in Aramaic, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.'
Then I asked, 'Who are you, Lord?' The Lord replied, 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.'
But get up and stand on your feet. I have appeared to you to appoint you as a servant and as a witness of what you have seen and will see of me.

I will rescue you from your own people and from the Gentiles. I am sending you to them to open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.

So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision. First to those in Damascus, then to those in Jerusalem and in all Judea, and then to the Gentiles, I preached that they should repent and turn to God and demonstrate their repentance by their deeds.
That is why the Jews seized me in the temple courts and tried to kill me.

But God has helped me to this very day; so I stand here and testify to small and great alike. I am saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen—that the Messiah would suffer and, as the first to rise from the dead, would bring the message of light to his own people and to the Gentiles.
At this point, Festus interrupted Paul’s defense. 'You are out of your mind, Paul!' he shouted.
'Your great learning is driving you insane.'
But Paul replied, 'I am not insane, most excellent Festus. What I am saying is true and reasonable.'
The king is familiar with these things, and I can speak freely to him. I am convinced that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.

Then Agrippa said to Paul, 'Do you think that in such a short time you can persuade me to be a Christian?' Paul replied, 'Short time or long—I pray to God that not only you but all who are listening to me today may become what I am, except for these chains.'
The king, the governor, Bernice, and those sitting with them stood up, and after they left, they began to say to one another, 'This man is not doing anything that deserves death or imprisonment.'
Agrippa said to Festus, 'This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.'
When it was decided that we would sail for Italy, Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion named Julius, who belonged to the Imperial Regiment.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium about to sail for ports along the coast of the province of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we landed at Sidon; and Julius, in kindness to Paul, allowed him to go to his friends so they might provide for his needs.

From there we put out to sea again and passed to the lee of Cyprus because the winds were against us. When we had sailed across the open sea off the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we landed at Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us on board.

We made slow headway for many days and had difficulty arriving off Cnidus. When the wind did not allow us to hold our course, we sailed by the south of Crete, opposite Salmone. We moved along the coast with difficulty and came to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea.
Much time had been lost, and sailing had already become dangerous because by now it was after the Day of Atonement.
So Paul warned them, 'Men, I can see that our voyage is going to be disastrous and bring great loss to ship and cargo, and to our own lives also.'
But the centurion, instead of listening to what Paul said, followed the advice of the pilot and the owner of the ship.
Since the harbor was unsuitable to winter in, the majority decided that we should sail on, hoping to reach Phoenix and winter there.
This was a harbor in Crete, facing both southwest and northwest.
When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had obtained what they wanted; so they weighed anchor and sailed along the shore of Crete.
Before very long, a wind of hurricane force, called the 'Northeaster,' swept down from the island.
The ship was caught by the storm and could not head into the wind; so we gave way to it and were driven along.
As we passed to the lee of a small island called Cauda, we were hardly able to make the lifeboat secure.

So the men hoisted it aboard, passed ropes under the ship itself to reinforce it, and fearing that they would run aground on the sandbars of Syrtis, they lowered the sea anchor and let the ship be driven along.
We took such a violent battering from the storm that the next day they began to throw the cargo overboard, and on the third day, they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands.
When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging, we finally gave up all hope of being saved.

After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up before them and said, 'Men, you should have taken my advice not to sail from Crete; then you would have spared yourselves this damage and loss.'
But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed.
Last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me and said, 'Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar.'
God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.
So keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God that it will happen just as he told me.
Nevertheless, we must run aground on some island.
On the fourteenth night we were still being driven across the Adriatic Sea, when about midnight the sailors sensed they were approaching land.
They took soundings and found that the water was a hundred and twenty feet deep. A short time later they took soundings again and found it was ninety feet deep.
Fearing that we would be dashed against the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight.

In an attempt to escape from the ship, the sailors let the lifeboat down into the sea, pretending they were going to lower some anchors from the bow. Then Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, 'Unless these men stay with the ship, you cannot be saved.'
So the soldiers cut the ropes that held the lifeboat and let it drift away.
Just before dawn Paul urged them all to eat. 'For the last fourteen days,' he said, 'you have been in constant suspense and have gone without food—you haven't eaten anything.'
Now I urge you to take some food. You need it to survive. Not one of you will lose a single hair from his head.
After he said this, he took some bread and gave thanks to God in front of them all. Then he broke it and began to eat.
They were all encouraged and ate some food themselves.
Altogether there were 276 of us on board.
When they had eaten as much as they wanted, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea.
When daylight came, they did not recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a sandy beach, where they decided to run the ship aground if they could.
Cutting loose the anchors, they left them in the sea and at the same time untied the ropes that held the rudders. Then they hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach.
But the ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast and would not move, but the stern was broken to pieces by the pounding of the surf.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to prevent any of them from swimming away and escaping.
But the centurion wanted to spare Paul's life and kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land.
The rest were to get there on planks or on other pieces of the ship.
In this way everyone reached land safely.
Once safely on shore, we found out that the island was called Malta.
The islanders showed us unusual kindness. They built a fire and welcomed us all because it was raining and cold.
Paul gathered a pile of brushwood and, as he put it on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened itself on his hand.
When the islanders saw the snake hanging from his hand, they said to each other, 'This man must be a murderer; for though he escaped from the sea, the goddess Justice has not allowed him to live.'
But Paul shook the snake off into the fire and suffered no ill effects.
The people expected him to swell up or suddenly fall dead, but after waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
There was an estate nearby that belonged to Publius, the chief official of the island.
He welcomed us to his home and showed us generous hospitality for three days.
His father was sick in bed, suffering from fever and dysentery.
Paul went in to see him and, after prayer, placed his hands on him and healed him.
When this had happened, the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured.
They honored us in many ways; and when we were ready to sail, they furnished us with the supplies we needed.
After three months we put out to sea in a ship that had wintered in the island—it was an Alexandrian ship with the figurehead of the twin gods Castor and Pollux.
We put in at Syracuse and stayed there three days.
From there we set sail and arrived at Rhegium. The next day the south wind came up, and on the following day we reached Puteoli.
There we found some brothers and sisters who invited us to spend a week with them. And so we came to Rome.
The believers there had heard that we were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of these people, Paul thanked God and was encouraged.
When we got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.

Three days later he called together the local Jewish leaders. When they had assembled, Paul said to them, 'My brothers, although I have done nothing against our people or against the customs of our ancestors, I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.'
They examined me and wanted to release me, because I was not guilty of any crime deserving death.
But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—not that I had any charge to bring against my own people.
For this reason I have asked to see you and talk with you. It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.'
They replied, 'We have not received any letters from Judea concerning you, and none of our people who have come from there has reported or said anything bad about you.'
But we want to hear what your views are, for we know that people everywhere are talking against this sect.

They arranged to meet Paul on a certain day, and came in even larger numbers to the place where he was staying. He witnessed to them from morning till evening, explaining about the kingdom of God, and from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets he tried to persuade them about Jesus.
Some were convinced by what he said, but others would not believe.

They disagreed among themselves and began to leave after Paul had made this final statement: 'The Holy Spirit spoke the truth to your ancestors when he said through Isaiah the prophet: Go to this people and say, 'You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving.' For this people’s heart has become calloused; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts and turn, and I would heal them.'
Therefore I want you to know that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!
When he said this, the Jews started arguing among themselves and left.
He lived in his own rented house for two full years, meeting everyone who came to him, and without any hindrance, he boldly preached the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.
The purpose of Paul writing the letter to the people of Rome was to pave the way for his visit to the church in Rome, which Paul had planned.
His plan was to work among the believers there for a short time and then, with their help, go to Spain.
In this book, we have found a complete summary of Paul's message.

After greeting the people of the church in Rome and telling them about his prayers for them, Paul mentions the main theme of this letter, because in this gospel, the righteousness of God is revealed by faith and for faith, (1:17).
Paul further explains this key point openly.
All of humanity, both Jews and Gentiles, needs to reconcile with God because all are equally under the influence of sin.
Through faith in Jesus Christ, people are reconciled with God.
Then Paul talks about the new life with Christ, which comes because of this new relationship with God.
The reconciliation that a believer has with God, and God's Spirit, frees them from the power of sin and death.
In chapters 5-8, Paul also discusses the purpose of God's law in the life of a believer and the power of God's Spirit.
Then the apostle grapples with the question of how both Jews and Gentiles can come into God's plan for all of humanity.

He concludes that the rejection of Jesus by the Jewish people is also a part of God's plan, which was designed to bring the entire human race into the grace of God in Jesus Christ, and he believes that the Jewish people will not remain turned away from Jesus forever.
Finally, Paul writes about how one should live the Christian life, especially loving others.
He takes these matters in the form of questions about the service of God, the kingdom, the duty of believers towards one another, and the conscience.
He concludes the letter with personal messages and praise to God.
This letter is from Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, chosen to be an apostle through God and set apart to proclaim His gospel.
Long before Jesus came into this world, God had promised that He would reveal this gospel through the prophets, which is written about in the Holy Scriptures.
This gospel is about the Son of God, who is our Lord Jesus Christ.
Physically, he was born of the lineage of King David, but by the power of the Holy Spirit, he was called the Son of God because he was raised from the dead.

Through Christ, we received grace and apostleship from God, so that for the sake of His name, Gentiles might believe in Christ and obey Him; you Gentile believers in Rome are among those whom God has called to be His people in Jesus Christ.
This letter is to all those in the city of Rome who are loved by God and have been called to be His holy people.
I pray that grace and peace may continue to be given to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Prayer of Thanksgiving: First of all, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith in Jesus Christ is being spoken of throughout the world.
God, whom I serve with all my heart and speak to people about concerning His Son's gospel, is my witness that I remember you all in my prayers at all times.
And I ask that, if possible, according to God's will, I may also come to visit you.
Because I long to see you, so that I may give you some spiritual gift to strengthen you in faith.
What I mean is that when I see you, you and I can encourage each other; you can be strengthened by knowing my faith, and I can be strengthened by knowing yours.

Beloved brothers, I want you to know that I have often planned to come to you so that I might see the same spiritual growth among you as I have seen among other Gentiles, but until now, I have been hindered.
I feel a burden in my heart to preach the word to those civilized people who know the Greek language and culture, to those who do not, and to both the wise and the foolish.
For this reason, I am eager to preach the gospel to you who live in the city of Rome as well.
The Power of the Gospel: Because I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ; God saves everyone through His power who believes in the gospel, first the Jews and then the Gentiles.
Because the gospel tells us how God makes us righteous in His sight.
Which is by faith in Christ from beginning to end, just as it is written in the Holy Scriptures, that the person who is made righteous by God in His sight will live by faith.
Humanity's Sin: God's wrath is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and wickedness of people; they suppress the truth of God by their wicked deeds.
They can know about God correctly and easily because God has told them about these things.

The truth is that from the beginning of the world, God's invisible qualities, His eternal power and His divinity, are in the world and are clearly seen, so people have no excuse that they do not know God.
Even knowing about God, they did not honor Him as God, nor did they thank Him.
Instead, they began to think vain thoughts about Him, and they did not think as they should have, but thought only of evil.
Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and did not glorify the immortal God, but instead worshipped images of mortal man, birds, crawling creatures, and four-footed animals.
For this reason, God gave them over to the evil desires of their hearts to do wrong things so that they might commit shameful acts with their bodies among themselves.
Because they believed a lie instead of the truth about God and worshipped and served created things, rather than the Creator who is forever worthy of glory! Amen.
That is why God gave them up to their shameful desires, causing even their women to exchange natural sexual relations for unnatural ones.
In the same way, the men left natural relations with women and began to burn with lust for one another, and men doing shameless acts with men brought the penalty upon themselves.
And since they did not think it worthwhile to know God, God gave them over to their depraved minds, so that they might do evil things.

That is why they became filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, greed, and malice, and full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice; they are gossips, slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to their parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, and merciless.
They know God's righteous decree that those who do such things deserve death, yet they not only do them themselves but also approve of those who practice them.
Therefore, my fellow believers, whoever you may be, you have no excuse; for when you judge others, you bring judgment upon yourself, because you who judge others do the very same things.
We know that God will judge those who do such evil things with righteousness.

When you judge those who do such things and you do the same, do you think that you will escape God's judgment? Do you despise the riches of God's kindness, tolerance, and patience? Do you not understand that God's kindness leads you to turn from sin? But you are stubborn and do not want to stop sinning, nor do you want to change yourself.
Therefore, on the day when God reveals His wrath, His judgment will be manifested with righteousness, and He will judge you severely.
God will give everyone according to what they have done.
To those who continue to do good and seek the glory, honor, and eternal life of God, God will give them eternal life.
But for those who are selfish and do not accept the truth, but obey wickedness, God's wrath and anger will fall upon them.
Trouble and distress will come upon every person.
God will judge the Jews first and then the people who are Gentiles.
But glory, honor, and peace will be given to everyone who does good, first the Jew and then those who are Gentiles.
Because God shows no partiality.

All those Gentiles who have sinned without knowing the laws and commandments that were given to the prophet Moses will also perish without knowing the laws, but those who sinned after knowing the laws will be judged according to the laws.
Because in God's sight, it is not those who hear the laws who are righteous, but it is the doers of the laws who will be made righteous.
Then when Gentiles who do not have the laws of the prophet Moses naturally follow the teachings of the laws, even without having the laws, they know what to do and what not to do.

They show the requirements of the laws written in their hearts, and their conscience also testifies to this, that this is true, because their thoughts either accuse them or tell them that they are doing what is right.
All this will be made clear on the day when God, according to the gospel preached through me, will judge the hidden matters of people through Jesus Christ.
Jews and the Laws: You call yourself a Jew and rely on the laws of the prophet Moses; God has mercy on you, which is why you have started to boast.
And you know the will of God; you desire the good things, because you have been taught these things through the laws of the prophet Moses.
And you are fully confident that you are a guide to the blind and a light of God for people lost in darkness.
And an instructor of the foolish and a teacher of children.
You know that the laws of God give you knowledge and truth in full.

Therefore, you who teach others, why don't you teach yourself? You preach, 'Do not steal,' do you not steal yourself? You who say, 'Do not commit adultery,' do you not commit adultery yourself? You who hate idols, do you not rob temples yourself? You who boast about knowing the laws, do you not dishonor God by not obeying the laws? 'Because of you Jews, God is spoken evil of among the Gentiles,' just as it is written in the Holy Scriptures.
